name: 160 Meter Band
transmit_note: Amateur license required (General/Advanced/Extra have full privileges; Technician has none on 160m).
practical_note: Primarily a night-time band; heavy static in summer thunderstorm season. Voice activity mostly above 1.840–1.900 MHz.
source_note: Band edges cross-checked via secondary source this session (FCC page blocked); voice/CW/phone sub-band splits and calling-frequency conventions are ARRL voluntary band-plan custom, not federal regulation.

name: 80/75 Meter Band
transmit_note: License required; Novice/Technician limited to 3.525–3.600 MHz CW only. General+ gets phone privileges roughly 3.800–4.000 MHz.
practical_note: Good regional night-time HF band; popular for regional nets and ragchews.
source_note: Band edges cross-checked via secondary source this session (FCC page blocked); voice/CW/phone sub-band splits and calling-frequency conventions are ARRL voluntary band-plan custom, not federal regulation.

name: 60 Meter Band (Channelized)
freq_range: 5330.5–5406.4 kHz (4 fixed channels + a lower-power secondary segment)
transmit_note: General/Advanced/Extra only. Channelized operation is mandatory (fixed dial frequencies, 1.5 kHz below each channel center for USB) - not a tunable band. Secondary user: must not interfere with US Government stations. Automatic operation is prohibited.
practical_note: 4 channel centers: 5332.0, 5348.0, 5373.0, 5405.0 kHz, plus a reduced-power secondary WRC-15 segment at 5351.5–5366.5 kHz. Rules here changed as recently as December 2025 - reverify current rules before any transmit use.
source_note: Recently and repeatedly revised regulation (power limits changed as recently as December 2025 per this session's cross-check) - treat as more likely to have changed since this was written than the other amateur bands.

name: 40 Meter Band
transmit_note: License required; Novice/Technician CW-only 7.025–7.125 MHz, General+ phone 7.125–7.300 MHz.
practical_note: Reliable regional/continental night-time HF band; one of the most consistently active ham HF bands after dark.
source_note: Band edges cross-checked via secondary source this session (FCC page blocked); voice/CW/phone sub-band splits and calling-frequency conventions are ARRL voluntary band-plan custom, not federal regulation.

name: 30 Meter Band
transmit_note: General/Advanced/Extra only; 200W PEP max. No phone (voice) permitted - CW and digital only, and no contests, by international agreement.
practical_note: Narrow shared band; mostly CW and FT8/other digital activity, rarely voice.
source_note: Band edges cross-checked via secondary source this session (FCC page blocked).

name: 20 Meter Band
transmit_note: License required; Technician has no phone privileges here. General+ gets 14.225–14.350 MHz phone (Extra gets more).
practical_note: The most popular HF DX (long-distance) band; often active worldwide nearly any time of day.
source_note: Band edges cross-checked via secondary source this session (FCC page blocked); voice/CW/phone sub-band splits and calling-frequency conventions are ARRL voluntary band-plan custom, not federal regulation.

name: 17 Meter Band
transmit_note: General/Advanced/Extra only.
practical_note: WARC band (no contests permitted); good daytime DX band.
source_note: Band edges cross-checked via secondary source this session (FCC page blocked); voice/CW/phone sub-band splits and calling-frequency conventions are ARRL voluntary band-plan custom, not federal regulation.

name: 15 Meter Band
transmit_note: License required; Technician CW-only 21.025–21.200 MHz, General+ phone 21.275–21.450 MHz.
practical_note: Daytime band, strongly tied to the solar/sunspot cycle - can be excellent or nearly dead depending on solar activity.
source_note: Band edges cross-checked via secondary source this session (FCC page blocked); voice/CW/phone sub-band splits and calling-frequency conventions are ARRL voluntary band-plan custom, not federal regulation.

name: 12 Meter Band
transmit_note: General/Advanced/Extra only.
practical_note: WARC band; narrow, daytime, solar-cycle dependent.
source_note: Band edges cross-checked via secondary source this session (FCC page blocked); voice/CW/phone sub-band splits and calling-frequency conventions are ARRL voluntary band-plan custom, not federal regulation.

name: 10 Meter Band
typical_receiver_mode: USB (voice); FM on the 29.5–29.7 MHz repeater segment
transmit_note: License required; Novice/Technician get limited phone privileges 28.300–28.500 MHz, General+ gets the full band.
practical_note: FM repeaters/simplex cluster near 29.520–29.680 MHz. Otherwise very solar-cycle dependent - can be nearly dead for years, then open worldwide during high solar activity.
source_note: Band edges cross-checked via secondary source this session (FCC page blocked); voice/CW/phone sub-band splits and calling-frequency conventions are ARRL voluntary band-plan custom, not federal regulation.

name: 6 Meter Band
typical_receiver_mode: USB near 50.125 MHz (weak-signal calling); FM in the upper portion
transmit_note: License required; all license classes have some 6m privileges.
practical_note: Nicknamed ‘the Magic Band’ - usually quiet, but sporadic-E and other propagation can unpredictably open it for long-distance contacts.
source_note: Band edges cross-checked via secondary source this session (FCC page blocked); voice/CW/phone sub-band splits and calling-frequency conventions are ARRL voluntary band-plan custom, not federal regulation.

name: 2 Meter Band
typical_receiver_mode: FM (repeaters/simplex); USB in the ~144.200 MHz weak-signal segment
transmit_note: License required; all classes, including Technician, have full 2m privileges - this is the most common entry-level ham VHF band.
practical_note: The most popular VHF ham band. National FM simplex calling frequency: 146.520 MHz. FM repeater outputs are commonly found across 144–148 MHz per local band plan.
source_note: Band edges cross-checked via secondary source this session; 146.520 MHz national simplex calling frequency is ARRL/community voluntary convention, not FCC regulation.

name: 1.25 Meter Band
transmit_note: License required, all classes; the 219–220 MHz segment is limited to fixed digital message-forwarding systems.
practical_note: Less common band - fewer radios support it. 222.100 MHz is a widely-used national simplex calling frequency in many regions.
source_note: Band edges cross-checked via secondary source this session (FCC page blocked).

name: 70 Centimeter Band
transmit_note: License required, all classes.
practical_note: Second most popular ham VHF/UHF band after 2m. National FM simplex calling frequency: 446.000 MHz. Widely used for repeaters and digital voice (DMR/D-STAR/System Fusion).
source_note: Band edges cross-checked via secondary source this session; 446.000 MHz national simplex calling frequency is voluntary convention, not FCC regulation.

name: AM Broadcast (Mediumwave)
freq_range: 535–1705 kHz (540–1700 kHz channelized, 10 kHz spacing, 117 channels)
transmit_note: Broadcasting requires an FCC broadcast station license - not for casual/personal transmission. This is a receive-only service for the public.
practical_note: AM travels far at night via skywave (ionospheric) propagation - distant stations often become audible after dark that are inaudible during the day.
source_note: Direct FCC page blocked (403); figure confirmed via an eCFR-citing secondary summary and is consistent across every independent reference checked - a long-stable, decades-unchanged allocation.

name: FM Broadcast
transmit_note: Broadcasting requires an FCC broadcast station license - not for casual/personal transmission. This is a receive-only service for the public.
practical_note: Line-of-sight VHF propagation - range is mostly limited by antenna height/terrain, not time of day (unlike AM).
source_note: Direct FCC page blocked (403); figure confirmed via an eCFR-citing secondary summary and is consistent across every independent reference checked - a long-stable, decades-unchanged allocation.

name: Shortwave Broadcast
transmit_note: International shortwave broadcasting requires government/international coordination - not for casual transmission. Receive-only for the public.
practical_note: Best reception varies a lot by band, time of day, and season - lower bands tend to favor night reception, higher bands favor daytime; all of it is sensitive to solar activity.
source_note: Meter-band ranges are ITU-coordinated international allocations; cross-checked via secondary source this session, not fetched directly from ITU.

channels.note: Most heavily used broadcast band historically; good year-round night reception.
Often the most active band overall; good night reception, seasonal in daytime.

name: NOAA Weather Radio (All Hazards)
transmit_note: NOAA/NWS transmitting stations only - receive-only for the public.
practical_note: Continuous weather broadcast plus All Hazards alerts (severe weather and some non-weather emergencies). Typical range ~40 miles from a full-power transmitter over level terrain. Coverage depends on the specific transmitter serving your location, not just your state. Channel numbering (WX1–WX7) is a common radio-manufacturer convention, not an official NOAA designation - confirm by frequency, not channel number.

name: Citizens Band (CB) Radio
typical_receiver_mode: AM (most common); USB for sideband-equipped radios
transmit_note: License-free since 1983. Power limited to 4W AM/FM, 12W PEP on SSB. Channel 9 is reserved for emergency/roadside-assistance use; Channel 19 is the common trucker/highway channel.
practical_note: Normally short-range ground-wave propagation (a few miles), but can skip long distances during sporadic-E or other solar/atmospheric conditions.
source_note: Direct FCC page blocked (403); numbers were cross-checked against multiple independent secondary sources that agreed exactly, and this channel plan is decades-stable/well-documented.

channels.note: Channels 23-24 are intentionally non-sequential in frequency (a historical CB band-plan quirk from when channels 22-23 were inserted later) - not an error.

name: FRS (Family Radio Service)
transmit_note: No individual license required. Power limits: channels 1-7 & 15-22 up to 2W, channels 8-14 up to 0.5W. All 22 channels are shared with GMRS.
practical_note: Real-world range is usually well under 1 mile in typical terrain, despite marketing claims of much longer range.
source_note: FCC page blocked (403) this session; table cross-checked via secondary source.

name: GMRS (General Mobile Radio Service)
freq_range: 462.550–467.725 MHz (22 shared channels + repeater input pairs on ch.15-22)
transmit_note: Requires a $35 FCC license (10-year term, no test required) covering the licensee's immediate family. Repeater use (channels 15-22) permitted up to 50W; channels 1-14 are simplex-only, shared with FRS at FRS power limits when used that way.
practical_note: Repeaters can extend usable range to roughly 20+ miles depending on antenna height/terrain. Per a 2024 FCC clarification, GMRS repeaters may not be linked to each other over the internet.
source_note: FCC page blocked (403) this session; cross-checked via secondary source. See the FRS entry for the shared channel table (channels 1-22 are identical frequencies).

name: MURS (Multi-Use Radio Service)
transmit_note: Licensed by rule - no individual FCC license needed. Power limited to 2W. External antennas are permitted (unlike FRS), subject to a height limit.
practical_note: Generally less crowded than FRS/GMRS in many areas; popular for trail, farm, and property use.
source_note: Numbers agreed exactly across two independent fetch attempts this session, despite the FCC page itself being blocked (403).

name: Marine VHF
transmit_note: Recreational vessels generally don't need an individual FCC license for domestic marine VHF use; commercial/passenger vessels and international voyages have separate licensing requirements. Channel 16 is for hailing/distress only - move to a working channel for conversation.
practical_note: Channel 16 = international distress/calling/safety. Channel 9 = recreational hailing (alternate to 16 in many areas). Channel 13 = bridge-to-bridge navigation safety. Channel 22A/1022 = USCG safety/weather announcements. Channel 70 = digital calling only, no voice.

channels.use: International distress, safety & calling - monitored by USCG
Bridge-to-bridge navigation safety; vessels >20m must monitor
USCG liaison & marine safety/weather broadcasts (announced first on ch.16)
Digital Selective Calling (DSC) only - no voice

name: Aviation / Airband
transmit_note: Aircraft/ground station radios operating under FAA/FCC rules - not for casual public transmission. Receive-only interest for most listeners.
practical_note: Deliberately uses AM, not FM - lets a stronger nearby signal be heard over a weaker one instead of one completely blocking the other ('capture effect'), which matters for safety. Standard US channel spacing is 25 kHz (8.33 kHz in parts of Europe). HF (2.850–22 MHz, USB) is used for oceanic/remote-area voice beyond VHF range.
source_note: Cross-checked via secondary reference this session (FAA/ICAO pages not directly fetched); band edges and the AM-mode convention are long-stable and globally consistent.

name: Railroad Radio
freq_range: approximately 159.6–161.6 MHz (exact lower edge unconfirmed - see note)
transmit_note: Licensed to railroads under FCC Part 90 - not for public transmission. Receive-only for the general public.
practical_note: Uses an AAR-coordinated channel plan (roughly 97 channels, 15 kHz spacing) for dispatch, road/yard operations, and defect detectors. Specific channel-to-railroad/purpose assignments are regional and change over time - consult a current regional scanner/railfan frequency guide for your area rather than relying on a fixed list here.
source_note: Three independent secondary sources gave three different lower band-edge figures (159.57 / 159.810 / 160.110 MHz) this session and no single clean authoritative public table was found. Range shown is approximate; no specific channel table is included by design - see docs/OPERATIONAL-DECISIONS.md.
